name: Konjo, coastal dialect as described, extended by the authors to mountain Konjo

catalog_locator: Sec. 7 'Stress', pp. 96-98; rule (70) Main Stress and rule (72) Secondary stress on p. 98; identity statement p. 71.
catalog_quote: [p. 96] Konjo has regular rule-governed stress. The regularities and apparent exceptions fit well within a straightforward statement. ... The first of the data sets above (60) illustrates the predominant case, that of roots being stressed on their penultimate syllable. The second ... in (61), shows forms that have an addition of a derivational affix that generally effects a shift in stress from the penultimate syllable of the root form to the penultimate syllable of the derived word. Then with (62) we find cases of inflectional endings that are generally clitics in Konjo. That is, the inflectional ending is not treated as existing for purposes of stress placement. [p. 98] (70) Main Stress: V ---> [1stress] / __ C0 <V C0>] <-vocative> (This rule says that a vowel receives primary stress when it occupies the penultimate syllable nucleus in a nonvocative utterance. When the form is vocative, the ultimate vowel is stressed.) The reflexes in the foregoing data sets depend crucially on the ordering Vowel Copy, Main Stress, Echo Vowel. When the last phonetic syllable(s) are clitic, they are not counted in determining the stress. ... (72) Secondary stress: ... (This rule puts a [2stress] on the first syllable of any word that is removed at least one syllable from the primary stress.)

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the word (root plus derivational suffixes; a derivational suffix moves stress to the new penult). Inflectional endings/enclitics (person markers, determiner -a, etc.) are outside the stress domain and not counted. Monosyllabic roots undergo Vowel Copy so that a penult exists. Surface antepenultimate stress arises only on consonant-final (/r l s/) roots that receive an echo vowel after stress assignment; vocatives take final stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Rule (72), p. 98: secondary stress on the first syllable of any word whose initial syllable is at least one syllable removed from the primary stress (e.g. [nàkupasíssekki]).
new_statements.exceptions: Antepenultimate stress on /r l s/-final roots via Echo Vowel (63); final stress in a few Dutch/Indonesian loans explained by vowel copy/declustering (65-67); prefixes never stressed (66); vocatives stressed on the ultima (68); clitic inflectional endings ignored (62).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level rule stated over root + derivational affixes; enclitics excluded (lexical-phonology strata). The description is based on Coastal Konjo fieldwork (Jannaya/Kalimporo, Kec. Kajang); p. 71 states mountain [= Highland] and coastal Konjo 'phonologies are nearly identical' and that the differences are lexical with 'only minor morphophonemic, morphological and syntactic differences'.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted source describes 'Konjo' from fieldwork in Jannaya/Kalimporo, Kec. Kajang, Kab. Bulukumba, i.e. Coastal Konjo (coas1295, ISO kjc). The authors, who surveyed the whole Makasar family in 1987-88 and themselves proposed the Highland/Coastal split, state on p. 71 that mountain [= Highland, high1275] and coastal Konjo 'phonologies are nearly identical' with 'only minor morphophonemic, morphological and syntactic differences'. No phonological description based on Highland Konjo (Konjo Pegunungan: W Sinjai, E Gowa highlands, N Bulukumba, S Bone) data was found anywhere (OLAC, Sulang, Garuda, LoC, Glottolog all list none). A catalog entry for high1275 should carry this extension caveat; the same file is the primary source for coas1295 (whose check folder is currently empty).

sources.note: Sec. 7 'Stress', pp. 96-98: regular rule-governed penultimate stress; derivational suffixes shift stress to the penult of the derived word; inflectional endings are clitics and are not counted; antepenultimate stress only on /r l s/-final roots via Echo Vowel; monosyllables get Vowel Copy to supply a penult; vocatives stressed on the final syllable; rule (70) Main Stress and rule (72) Secondary stress (first syllable) on p. 98. p. 71: notes reflect Coastal Konjo (fieldwork in Kajang) but mountain [Highland] and coastal Konjo 'phonologies are nearly identical'.
